drapeaux.note: The last sentence of the French contrasts the “20th-century geology” with the excavators of 1900, but the geological study it refers to was published in 2001 (work done in the late 1990s). Translated as written; “20th-century” may be meant as “modern”.

titre: The Pythia of Delphi and the Underground Vapors Hypothesis
accroche: Throughout the 20th century, archaeologists judged the vapor that sent the Pythia into a trance to be invented. A 2001 geological study reopens the case.
contenu_vulgarise:
For more than a thousand years, from the 8th century BCE to the 4th century CE, Greek cities and then Rome sent their most sensitive political and military questions to a woman seated on a tripod, in the dim light of an underground chamber of the temple of Apollo at Delphi. Ancient authors (Plutarch, Strabo, Diodorus Siculus) report that a vapor rose from a fissure in the ground and sent the Pythia into a trance before she delivered her oracles, often obscure, sometimes cutting.

## A Story Believed to Be Invented

When French archaeologists excavated the site between 1892 and 1903, they found no gaping fissure, no cavern beneath the oracular chamber. Throughout the 20th century, the dominant scholarly explanation therefore became that the ancients had invented the vapor: the trance would be an effect of collective autosuggestion, the fissure a legend with no geological basis, to be filed with the other marvelous elements of the ancient account.

An interdisciplinary team (the geologist Jelle de Boer (Wesleyan University), the archaeologist John Hale (University of Louisville), and the geochemist Jeffrey Chanton (Florida State University)) took up the case in the late 1990s and published in 2001, in the journal *Geology*, an unexpected result: two active faults, one running east-west, the other northwest-southeast, cross exactly beneath the supposed location of the oracular chamber. The subsoil there is a bituminous limestone whose hydrocarbon content reaches up to 20%. In the water of the nearby spring, the team detected traces of light gases (ethylene, methane, ethane), brought up through fissures that earthquakes periodically reopen: the one nobody had found may simply have been more active two thousand years ago than it is today.

## What This Changes

Ethylene draws particular attention: at low doses, earlier work in anesthesiology had shown that it produces a light conscious trance, able to respond coherently to questions (the register that most ancient oracles describe), while at a higher dose it produces a loss of control of the limbs, close to the single ancient account of a Pythia seized by violent convulsions, who died a few days after her session.

The case is nevertheless not closed: specialists of the ancient world, including the classicist Daryn Lehoux, dispute the chemical reading, judging the required gas concentration improbable and the identification of certain compounds in the samples uncertain. What this case shifts is therefore not the certainty of having finally “explained” the oracle, but the very meaning of skepticism: it is no longer antiquity that is accused of having imagined a nonexistent fissure; it is 20th-century geology that must now convince the specialists in antiquity that it has indeed found the one the excavators of 1900 had looked for in the wrong place.

repere.texte: In 2001, a team of geologists detected in the water of the Kerna spring, at Delphi, traces of ethylene (0.3 parts per million), methane (15.3 ppm), and ethane (0.2 ppm), brought up by two active faults that cross beneath the oracular chamber of the temple of Apollo, in a limestone subsoil whose hydrocarbon content reaches up to 20%.
repere.source: de Boer, Hale, and Chanton, Geology, vol. 29, 2001; Wikipedia, “Pythia”

carte.punch: The Pythia's vapors, judged invented, really did rise from a geological fault.
carte.idee: For a century, archaeologists believed that the vapor inspiring the Pythia of Delphi was a legend. In 2001, a geological study found two active faults and hydrocarbon gases beneath the temple of Apollo. The hypothesis remains debated, but it has reopened a case thought to be closed.

quiz.question: What does the 2001 geological study change relative to the 20th-century scientific position on the Delphic oracle?
choix: It proves that the Pythia invented her oracles with no substance involved
It establishes with certainty that ethylene alone explains all the trances reported by ancient authors
It identifies faults and hydrocarbon gases beneath the temple, reopening a case that the excavations of 1900 had filed as legend
It demonstrates that the site of Delphi never housed an underground oracular chamber
quiz.explication: The 2001 study found active faults and traces of hydrocarbon gases beneath the temple, which reopened a case filed as legend since the excavations of 1892-1903, but the conclusion remains debated among specialists, and nothing indicates that all the trances are explained by this single mechanism, that the Pythia invented her oracles, or that the site did not house an underground chamber.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the French archaeologists who excavated Delphi from 1892 to 1903 find beneath the oracular chamber?
choix: An active fissure from which vapors were still escaping
No gaping fissure, no cavern beneath the oracular chamber
A network of galleries dug to diffuse gases
The remains of a second temple built over the spring
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The excavators found no fissure, which established for the whole 20th century the idea that the vapor of the ancient authors was an invention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does ethylene draw particular attention in this hypothesis?
choix: At low doses, it produces a light conscious trance compatible with the account of the oracles
At any dose, it produces a deep sleep that prevents answering
It is the only gas the team detected in the spring water
It acts only on animals and never on human beings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Work in anesthesiology showed that at a low dose it produces a trance in which one answers coherently, and that at a higher dose it causes loss of control of the limbs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the classicist Daryn Lehoux object to in the chemical reading of the trance?
choix: That it ignores the texts of Plutarch, Strabo, and Diodorus
That it denies that Delphi ever hosted an oracle
That it judges the required gas concentration improbable and the identification of certain compounds uncertain
That it assumes the site's faults are too old to have been active
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The criticisms concern the gas concentration required and the identification of certain compounds: the case is therefore not closed, despite the 2001 study.
